questions.question: State major engineering problems in Freush process.
questions.solution_html:
• Large amounts of heat are needed to generate superheated water (around 160 –170°C) to
  • melt underground sulfur, making the process energy-intensive and costly.
  • Drilling and maintaining concentric pipes (three -pipe system) deep underground is
  • difficult, and corrosion or mechanical failure can occur due to high temperature and
  • pressure.
  • Significant heat is lost to surrounding rock formations, reducing efficiency and requiring
  • continuous heating to keep sulfur molten.
  • Proper control of compressed air and molten sulfur flow is challenging; fluctuations can
  • reduce recovery efficiency or cause operational hazards.
  • The process is only suitable for sulfur deposits located under impermeable layers and at
  • certain depths, restricting its use.
  • Possible groundwater contamination and land subsidence can occur if the operation is not
  • properly managed. (Any 4 Points give 4marks)

  • polyester, and polyethylene.

questions.question: Outline emulsion polymerization with its components.
questions.solution_html:
• properties, and applications of polystyrene.
  • Polystyrene is manufactured by bulk polymerization (mass polymerization) using styrene
  • monomer. In this method, pure styrene is taken in a reactor along with a small amount of initiator
  • such as benzoyl peroxide. The mixture is heated to about 80–150°C in the absence of solvent. The
  • initiator decomposes to form free radicals, which initiate chain polymerization of styrene. As the
  • reaction proceeds, viscosity increases and the polymer is formed. The process is carried out in
  • stages to control heat and avoid a uto-acceleration. Finally, the molten polymer is cooled and
  • solidified to obtain polystyrene.
  • The reaction can be represented as: n CH₂=CH–C₆H₅ →ₙ
  • Preparation steps: Initially, purified styrene monomer is mixed with an initiator. The mixture is
  • heated gradually in a reactor under controlled temperature and pressure. Polymerization begins
  • with free radical formation and continues with chain propagatio n. The increasing viscosity is
  • managed by stepwise heating. After completion, the polymer is cooled, extruded, and cut into
  • granules for commercial use.
  • Properties: Polystyrene is a transparent, rigid, and lightweight thermoplastic with good
  • dimensional stability. It has excellent electrical insulating properties and is resistant to acids and
  • alkalis but is attacked by organic solvents. It is brittle in nature and has low impact strength, though
  • it can be modified (as high-impact polystyrene). It softens on heating and can be easily moulded.
  • Applications: Polystyrene is widely used in the manufacture of disposable cups, plates, and
  • packaging materials (thermocol/expanded polystyrene). It is used for electrical insulation, toys
  • household items, laboratory ware, and as foam for thermal insulation in refrigerators and buildings.
  • Thus, due to its ease of processing, low cost, and useful properties, polystyrene has extensive
  • commercial applications. (2.5 marks each for bulk polymerisation and preparation step 5 marks
  • each for properties and applications)

questions.question: Describe the advantages and applications of transfer moulding.
questions.solution_html:
• Transfer moulding is a method used mainly for moulding thermosetting plastics, where the
  • material is first heated in a chamber and then transferred into a closed mould cavity. This process
  • offers several advantages, such as better surface finish and dimens ional accuracy compared to
  • compression moulding, as the material flows uniformly into the mould. It is suitable for moulding
  • complex shapes and intricate designs, including inserts like metal components, as it ensures proper
  • encapsulation. The process also reduces internal stresses, minimizes material wastage, and
  • provides improved mechanical properties in the final product.
  • The applications of transfer moulding are mainly found in the electrical and electronics industries
  • for manufacturing components such as switches, circuit breakers, connectors, and encapsulated
  • coils. It is also used in the production of automotive parts, appliance components, and moulded
  • items requiring high precision and good surface finish. Thus, transfer moulding is widely preferred
  • for producing high-quality, detailed thermosetting plastic products.
  • (3 points from advantages and applications give 3.5 marks)

questions.question: Describe preparation, properties, and uses of nitroethane, 1-nitropropane and 2-nitropropane.
questions.solution_html:
• Nitroalkanes such as nitroethane, 1-nitropropane, and 2-nitropropane are prepared by treating alkyl
  • halides with silver nitrite (AgNO₂) . C₂H₅X + AgNO₂ → C₂H₅NO₂ + AgX (nitroethane)
  • C₃H₇X + AgNO₂ → C₃H₇NO₂ + AgX (nitropropanes, giving both 1- and 2-isomers).
  • These compounds exhibit characteristic properties due to the presence of the electron
  • withdrawing –NO₂ group. They are polar, have relatively high boiling points, and are moderately
  • soluble in water but highly soluble in organic solvents. Primary nitroalka nes (nitroethane and 1
  • nitropropane) show tautomerism (nitro –aci form) and are acidic in nature, whereas secondary
  • nitroalkanes (2-nitropropane) are less acidic. They undergo reactions such as reduction to amines

  • In terms of uses, nitroethane is used as a solvent, fuel additive, and intermediate in organic

questions.question: Describe the manufacture of polystyrene by bulk polymerisation. Explain the preparation steps, properties, and applications of polystyrene.
questions.solution_html:
• Polystyrene is manufactured by bulk polymerization (mass polymerization) using styrene
  • monomer. In this method, pure styrene is taken in a reactor along with a small amount of initiator
  • such as benzoyl peroxide. The mixture is heated to about 80–150°C in the absence of solvent. The
  • initiator decomposes to form free radicals, which initiate chain polymerization of styrene. As the
  • reaction proceeds, viscosity increases and the polymer is formed. The process is carried out in
  • stages to control heat and avoid a uto-acceleration. Finally, the molten polymer is cooled and
  • solidified to obtain polystyrene.
  • The reaction can be represented as: n CH₂=CH–C₆H₅ →ₙ
  • Preparation steps: Initially, purified styrene monomer is mixed with an initiator. The mixture is
  • heated gradually in a reactor under controlled temperature and pressure. Polymerization begins
  • with free radical formation and continues with chain propagatio n. The increasing viscosity is
  • managed by stepwise heating. After completion, the polymer is cooled, extruded, and cut into
  • granules for commercial use.
  • Properties: Polystyrene is a transparent, rigid, and lightweight thermoplastic with good
  • dimensional stability. It has excellent electrical insulating properties and is resistant to acids and
  • alkalis but is attacked by organic solvents. It is brittle in nature and has low impact strength, though
  • it can be modified (as high-impact polystyrene). It softens on heating and can be easily moulded.
  • Applications: Polystyrene is widely used in the manufacture of disposable cups, plates, and
  • packaging materials (thermocol/expanded polystyrene). It is used for electrical insulation, toys
  • household items, laboratory ware, and as foam for thermal insulation in refrigerators and buildings.
  • Thus, due to its ease of processing, low cost, and useful properties, polystyrene has extensive
  • commercial applications. (2.5 marks each for bulk polymerisation and preparation step 5 marks
  • each for properties and applications)

  • tensile strength, good thermal stability, excellent chemical resistance, and resistance to sunlight
  • and weathering. It also has good fibre -forming ability due to strong intermolecular interactions
  • between nitrile groups, resulting in closely packed, crystalline structures.

  • environmental degradation. In filtration membranes, PAN’s chemic al resistance and stability

  • thermal stability and re sistance to chemicals, and it is also used as a precursor for carbon fibres
  • which are widely used in protective clothing, aerospace components, and high-strength materials.
  • Thus, the combination of strength, stability, and chemical resistance makes PAN su itable for
